implementation_notes: The cats documentation states the trade-off directly: an Either for-comprehension is fail-fast and surfaces only the first violation, while Validated is an applicative - (checkA, checkB, checkC).mapN(build) accumulates every Invalid into a NonEmptyChain (ValidatedNec) and yields one Validated value the caller inspects. Choose it when the validations are independent and the project already depends on cats; keep fail-fast Either where a later check needs the earlier value.
pitfalls: Validated is not a monad - it has no flatMap, so a for-comprehension over it does not compile; use mapN/traverse and convert to Either for dependent checks.
mapN needs an implicit Applicative (and a Semigroup for the error type with plain Validated[E, A]); the Nec aliases supply the Semigroup for you.
The error side is a NonEmptyChain, so it must be mapped to the API's list/array form explicitly at the boundary.

variants.name: hand-written Notification buffer
variants.implementation_notes: Without cats the pattern is written directly: a Notification holding a ListBuffer of violations with add/hasErrors/errors, passed into each check, and the caller reads errors once to decide. It keeps the domain free of a functional-effects dependency and is the form teams pick when the validation is procedural (config loading, batch import) rather than a pure pipeline.
pitfalls: Returning the ListBuffer itself would let callers mutate the notification; expose a copied List from the accessor.
Sharing one Notification between futures or actors reintroduces the concurrency bug the accumulation was meant to avoid - keep it per call.
Capturing the Notification in a closure instead of passing it explicitly makes the validator untestable in isolation.
